Choose the rendering path

One canvas, several ways to draw

The decision

The central question is not “Can Power BI render it?” It is “How much interaction, control, and operational complexity does it need?”

Press Space to walk through the choices.

01 · Start here

Built-in visuals

Power BI’s native charts already provide filtering, highlighting, tooltips, themes, accessibility, export, and responsive layout. Formatting, DAX, field parameters, small multiples, and custom tooltip pages can stretch them further than their defaults suggest.

Interaction

Fully participates in Power BI selections, cross-filtering, drill behavior, and report themes.

Use it when

The visual grammar is conventional and configuration can express the story without custom rendering code.

Useful extension

DAX-generated SVG can add icons, status marks, sparklines, and compact diagrams to tables and matrices.

Tradeoff

You work within Microsoft’s layouts and interaction patterns; unusual visual forms quickly reach their limits.

Native interactionLowest maintenanceBest governance
02 · Ready-made

AppSource + organizational visuals

Install a packaged visual from Microsoft AppSource or let an administrator distribute approved visuals through the organization. Technically, these use the same custom visual framework as a visual you build yourself—the code and packaging have simply been supplied for you.

Interaction

Can support selection, filtering, highlighting, formatting, and tooltips when the visual’s author implements them.

Use it when

A maintained visual already solves the problem and its license, support model, and design fit the report.

Distribution

Choose certified AppSource visuals for additional Microsoft testing, or publish internal visuals through the organizational library.

Tradeoff

Behavior, update cadence, data access, and long-term support depend on the publisher and your tenant policy.

ReusableGoverned distributionMinimal development
03 · Declarative

Vega and Vega-Lite

A visual such as Deneb lets you describe a bespoke chart with a Vega or Vega-Lite specification. You control marks, scales, axes, layering, and data transformations without creating an entire TypeScript project.

Interaction

Supports many Power BI selections and tooltips through the host visual, within the features its implementation exposes.

Use it when

The design is unusual but still expressible as a two-dimensional grammar of marks, encodings, and transformations.

What it really is

This is an authoring shortcut built on the custom visual framework, rather than a separate Power BI rendering engine.

Tradeoff

Complex specifications can become difficult to maintain, and application-like or 3D experiences remain outside its sweet spot.

Less codeFine visual controlSpecification-driven
04 · Analytical

Python and R visuals

Power BI sends the assigned fields to a dataframe, runs your script, and captures the resulting plot as an image. This opens mature statistical, scientific, forecasting, and machine-learning libraries without requiring a custom web visual.

Interaction

The image rerenders when report filters change, but clicking a plotted mark cannot select data or cross-filter another visual.

Use it when

The analysis or specialized chart already exists in Python or R and static output is acceptable.

Service reality

Power BI Service controls runtime versions, supported packages, execution time, data size, and network access.

Tradeoff

You lose native tooltips, selection behavior, accessibility semantics, and the fluid responsiveness of a web-rendered visual.

Specialized librariesStatic imagePackage limits
💪 05 · Maximum control

Custom visual SDK

Build a .pbiviz package with TypeScript or JavaScript and use the browser platform to create almost any visual experience. Power BI provides the data, viewport, formatting settings, theme, tooltip services, and selection manager; your code owns the interface and rendering.

Interaction

Can initiate selections and cross-filtering, respond to report filters, expose Format-pane controls, and integrate native tooltips.

Use it when

The visual form or interaction is the product and existing charts, specifications, or script-generated images cannot express it.

Browser freedom

Use HTML, CSS, SVG, Canvas, WebGL, animation, layout, interaction libraries, or any compatible browser-based capability.

Tradeoff

You own data mapping, resizing, formatting, accessibility, performance, packaging, testing, and future compatibility.

Full browser platformPower BI APIsCustom interactionReusable package
06 · Take action

Power Apps visual

Embed a canvas application inside the report and pass selected report data into it. The result can edit records, capture comments, request approvals, or start an operational workflow alongside the analysis.

Interaction

Receives report context and supports application behavior, but it does not behave like a native chart or general rendering engine.

Use it when

The user must act on what the report reveals: correct a record, submit a decision, or write data back.

Strength

Joins analytical context to forms, connectors, business rules, and existing Power Platform workflows.

Tradeoff

It brings a separate application lifecycle, permissions model, connection setup, and performance profile.

OperationalFormsWriteback
07 · Beyond the canvas

Power BI Embedded

Embed an entire report inside a custom web application. The surrounding application can use any web technology and coordinate its state with Power BI through the embedding APIs.

Interaction

The host application can control report pages, filters, bookmarks, and events while presenting its own interface around the report.

Use it when

The report belongs inside a larger customer portal, product, or guided workflow that needs a completely custom shell.

Freedom

Place D3, Three.js, React, maps, navigation, and application data beside Power BI without visual-sandbox constraints.

Tradeoff

The visualization is outside the PBIX canvas, and your application owns authentication, deployment, layout, and state synchronization.

Custom applicationEmbedding APIsTotal freedom

A brief history of web visualization

Mike Bostock

Portrait: Mike Bostock / Observable

Visualization toolmaker

He helped give data a native language on the web.

Mike Bostock is a visualization researcher, designer, and software developer. He created D3, previously helped develop Protovis at Stanford, and worked as a graphics editor at The New York Times. His work joins software design with a newsroom instinct: build an interface that helps a reader understand something complicated.

StanfordVisualization Group and Protovis
2011D3: Data-Driven Documents
2012–2015New York Times Graphics
LaterFounder of Observable
Sources: Observable profile · bost.ocks.org
The newsroom as a laboratory

Explanations you can explore

These projects were collaborations. Bostock’s role joined data, code, interaction, and relentless visual iteration.

2009 · Stanford Visualization Group

Protovis made graphics declarative.

Protovis described a visualization as data-driven marks—bars, dots, lines, areas, labels, and wedges. Instead of looping through data and drawing each shape, an author declared how data should control position, size, and color.

The ideaCompose charts from graphical marks rather than fixed chart types.
The toolsScales, layouts, panels, inheritance, interaction, and SVG output.
The limitIts own scene graph sat between the author and the browser.
Protovisdata → marks
Source: Protovis project · Final release 3.3.1; retired in favor of D3 in 2011
2011 · Data-Driven Documents

D3 removed the wall between data and the browser.

D3 binds data directly to document elements and lets the browser render the result. It supplies selections, data joins, scales, shapes, layouts, geography, transitions, and interaction—then leaves the final form to the author.

Native mediumWork directly with HTML, SVG, CSS, Canvas, events, and browser tools.
Core patternJoin data to elements, then create, update, or remove only what changed.
The tradeoffExtraordinary freedom in exchange for more design and engineering decisions.
DataDOMBrowser
D3bind · transform · render
Source: d3js.org · Bostock, Ogievetsky & Heer, “D3: Data-Driven Documents”

D3 primitives in motion

Small pieces, expressive systems

Each example combines a few focused modules. The code is representative; the visualization is rendered live with D3.

Select · modify · animate

Selections

Select browser elements and set visual properties from data.

const dots = svg
  .selectAll("circle")
  .data(data)
  .join("circle");

dots.transition()
  .attr("cx", d => x(d.value))
  .attr("cy", d => y(d.group))
  .attr("r",  d => size(d.amount))
  .attr("fill", d => color(d.group));
Live D3
Enter · update · exit

Data joins

Keep the document synchronized as data appears, persists, and disappears.

letters
  .data(randomLetters(), d => d)
  .join(
    enter => enter.append("text")
      .attr("fill", "#2f9d62"),
    update => update
      .attr("fill", "#17201f"),
    exit => exit
      .attr("fill", "#c4473a")
      .call(exit => exit.transition().remove())
  );
Green enters · red exitsInspired by selection.join
Domain → range

Scales

Translate abstract values into position, size, color, or any other visual property.

const position = d3.scaleLinear()
  .domain([0, 100])
  .range([80, width - 60]);

const size = d3.scaleSqrt()
  .domain([0, 100])
  .range([5, 28]);

const color = d3.scaleLinear()
  .domain([0, 50, 100])
  .range(["rust", "teal", "plum"]);
A visual translation machine
Scales made legible

Axes

Turn invisible mappings into reference marks that readers can interpret.

const x = d3.scaleTime()
  .domain(d3.extent(data, d => d.date))
  .range([margin.left, width]);

const y = d3.scaleLinear()
  .domain([0, d3.max(data, d => d.value)])
  .nice()
  .range([height, margin.top]);

gx.call(d3.axisBottom(x));
gy.call(d3.axisLeft(y));
Ticks establish meaning
Data → path geometry

Shapes

Generators turn the same values into lines, areas, arcs, symbols, and radial forms.

const line = d3.line()
  .x(d => x(d.x))
  .y(d => y(d.y))
  .curve(d3.curveCatmullRom);

const area = d3.area()
  .x(d => x(d.x))
  .y0(height)
  .y1(d => y(d.y));

const arcs = d3.pie()(values)
  .map(d3.arc().innerRadius(42));
One dataset · many forms
Hierarchy → enclosure

Treemap layout

A layout computes rectangles; selections decide how those rectangles look and move.

const root = d3.hierarchy(data)
  .sum(d => d.value)
  .sort((a, b) => b.value - a.value);

d3.treemap()
  .size([width, height])
  .paddingInner(3)(root);

cells.data(root.leaves(), d => d.data.name)
  .join("rect")
  .attr("x", d => d.x0)
  .attr("width", d => d.x1 - d.x0);
Values continuously reshape the whole
Forces → emergent position

Force-directed network

Nodes settle into a layout through a simulation of links, charge, collision, and centering.

const simulation = d3.forceSimulation(nodes)
  .force("link", d3.forceLink(links)
            .id(d => d.id).distance(65))
  .force("charge", d3.forceManyBody())
  .force("collide", d3.forceCollide(16))
  .on("tick", draw);

nodes.call(d3.drag()
  .on("start", dragstarted)
  .on("drag", dragged)
  .on("end", dragended));
A layout that finds itself
Sphere → screen → cells

Projection + Voronoi

Project geographic coordinates, then use computational geometry to divide the visible map.

const projection = d3.geoNaturalEarth1()
  .fitExtent([[20, 20], [width - 20, height - 20]],
    {type: "Sphere"});

const points = places.map(d => projection(d));
const delaunay = d3.Delaunay.from(points);
const voronoi = delaunay.voronoi(
  [0, 0, width, height]
);

cells.attr("d", (_, i) =>
  voronoi.renderCell(i));
Natural Earth + rotating Voronoi

From idea to .pbiviz

Building a custom visual

01 · Prepare

Install the toolchain

A custom visual is a TypeScript web project compiled and packaged for Power BI.

npm install -g powerbi-visuals-tools@latest
pbiviz new myVisual
Local tools

Node.js, npm, an editor, and the pbiviz command-line tools.

Power BI

Desktop for packaged testing; the Service and Developer mode for the fastest live loop.

Node.jsVS CodepbivizPower BI
02 · Declare

Define the contract

├─ capabilities.jsonData roles, mappings, formatting properties, and privileges.
├─ pbiviz.jsonIdentity, API version, metadata, and entry points.
├─ package.jsonDependencies and build scripts.
├─ src/TypeScript source.
│  ├─ visual.tsIVisual implementation and rendering lifecycle.
│  └─ settings.tsFormat-pane settings model.
├─ style/Visual styles.
│  └─ visual.lessStyles compiled into the package.
└─ assets/Packaged static assets.
   └─ icon.png20 × 20 Visualizations-pane icon.
03 · Implement

Implement IVisual

export class Visual implements IVisual {constructor(options: VisualConstructorOptions) {// Create elements and retain Power BI host services.}
public update(options: VisualUpdateOptions): void {// Read the current state and render the visual.}
public getFormattingModel(): FormattingModel {// Return the controls shown in the Format pane.return this.formattingModel;}}
04 · Develop

Test live in the Service

pbiviz start
Developer mode

Enable it in Power BI Service, add the Developer visual, and assign report fields.

Fast feedback

Edit and save locally; the development server rebuilds and reloads the visual.

Remember

localhost:8080 serves visual assets. It is not a standalone preview page.

Exercise the host

Resize, filter, cross-highlight, change formatting, and test incomplete field assignments.

Live reloadReal report dataHost interactions
05 · Package

Build the portable visual

pbiviz package
→ dist/myVisual.pbiviz
Desktop or Service

Visualizations pane → ellipsis → Import a visual from a file.

One distributable

The package contains the compiled code, styles, manifest, icon, and local assets.

Static build

A packaged visual does not live-reload. Repackage and reimport after changes.

Final check

Test the packaged build as well as the Developer visual before distributing it.

.pbivizDesktopService

Power BI host integrations

Choose how native the visual feels

01 · Selections

Give every mark an identity

Create a SelectionId for each meaningful element and send it through ISelectionManager.

Clicked mark
→
SelectionId
→
Power BI host
The visual owns

Identity creation, selected styling, clearing, and multi-select behavior.

The host owns

The shared report selection and communication with every other visual.

02 · Cross-filtering and cross-highlighting

One selection, three responses

Report authors decide how each target responds; the source visual initiates the selection.

Selection
→
Filter
Highlight
None
Cross-filter

Targets receive only matching data and redraw around the reduced result.

Cross-highlight

Targets retain the full context and receive highlighted values to emphasize.

03 · Filter APIs

Act like a slicer

applyJsonFilter() changes persistent report filter state rather than creating a temporary selection.

Custom control
→
JSON filter
→
Semantic model
→
All visuals
Filter shapes

Basic, advanced, tuple, identity, and hierarchical identity filters.

Restore state

Read active filters from options.jsonFilters on subsequent updates.

04 · Bookmark support

Return to the saved view

Power BI captures the visual’s selection or filter state and later asks the visual to restore it.

Selection or filter
→
Report bookmark
→
Restored visual
Selection visual

Register a Selection Manager callback and repaint the restored identities.

Filter visual

Read the restored JSON filter and rebuild the control’s visible state.

05 · Native tooltips

Let Power BI render the detail

Use ITooltipService to show report-aware information at the pointer or touch location.

Hover + SelectionId
→
Tooltip service
→
Native or report-page tooltip
Native behavior

Show, move, and hide tooltips using the report’s familiar presentation.

Richer context

Support multiple values, report-page tooltips, and modern drill actions.

06 · Context menus

Preserve the right-click contract

Call showContextMenu() with the pointer position and, when available, the clicked data identity.

Empty space
Data point
→
Power BI menu
Visual context

Expose the standard menu when users right-click the visual background.

Data context

Add Include, Exclude, and Show data as a table for identified marks.

07 · Drill-down and hierarchies

Move through levels of meaning

Declare drillable grouping roles, consume hierarchy levels, and coordinate with the host’s drill controls.

Era
→
Period
→
Series
→
Stage
User-driven

Support drill down, drill up, next level, and expand-to-next-level behavior.

Visual-driven

The Drilldown API can request a drill operation programmatically.

08 · Complete integration

The rest of the host surface

Formatting + persistenceFormat pane, on-object formatting, and saved visual properties.
Themes + high contrastReport color palettes and accessible system colors.
Keyboard + screen readersFocus management, ARIA semantics, and accessible navigation.
Large dataSegmented and incremental loading with fetchMoreData().
Sorting + localizationSemantic sorting and translated interface strings.
Rendering + focus modesRender events and view, edit, advanced-edit, and focus states.
Authoring experienceLanding pages and direct formatting of selected elements.
Privileged servicesDownloads, storage, web access, authentication, URLs, and dialogs.

What we learned

A custom visual is a choice

01
Choose the right rendering path

Use the simplest Power BI option that can express the experience the report needs.

02
D3 composes small primitives

Selections, joins, scales, shapes, layouts, and geography combine into expressive systems.

03
The project is a contract

Capabilities declare the data; IVisual turns each Power BI update into an interface.

04
Native behavior is deliberate

Selections, filters, bookmarks, tooltips, and drill-down only work when the visual participates.

Start with the story. Add complexity only where it earns its place.
